name: Chiropractic neck adjustment

card.summary: High-velocity neck manipulation sometimes sought for posture and jaw or face alignment; case reports link it to arterial injury and stroke.
card.note: Case reports describe vertebral artery dissection and other serious complications after neck manipulation.

quick.overview:
A chiropractic neck adjustment is a thrust applied to the joints of the neck, usually by a chiropractor. In looksmaxxing and related fringe circles it is sometimes discussed as a way to correct posture or alignment thought to affect the face.

Research on cervical manipulation concerns neck pain, not appearance, and its safety is debated. Published case reports describe stroke and eye bleeding after neck manipulation.
quick.mechanism: A quick, small-amplitude thrust is applied to a cervical joint, often producing a popping sound. Practitioners say it restores joint movement. Reviewers describe the evidence for effect as limited and the degree of serious risk as uncertain.
quick.risks: The main concern is vertebral artery dissection, which can lead to stroke. A 2001 study reported higher rates of vertebrobasilar stroke in adults under 45 who had recently visited a chiropractor, with no significant association over 45. Some chiropractors dispute a causal link.

lead: A chiropractic neck adjustment, or cervical spinal manipulation, is a thrust technique applied to the joints of the neck. It is used for neck pain and is also discussed in appearance-related communities in connection with posture and head alignment.

A 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence on spinal manipulation for neck pain, while a smaller body of moderate-to-low-quality evidence suggests multiple sessions may improve pain and function compared with some medications [1]. No study identified for this article evaluates neck manipulation for facial appearance.

The central safety concern is vertebral artery dissection. Case reports describe cerebellar infarction after a chiropractor's neck manipulation [2] and preretinal hemorrhages after high-velocity low-amplitude cervical manipulation [3].

paras: A 2015 Cochrane review found no high-quality evidence for spinal manipulation in neck pain, and a 2007 review reported moderate-to-high-quality evidence of benefit for chronic neck pain not caused by whiplash [1]. Effectiveness for facial or postural appearance has not been studied.

Reviewers describe little evidence of harm and little evidence of safety, and note that under-reporting is likely substantial [1]. A survey of British neurologists found 35 cases of serious neurological complications after cervical manipulation that had not been reported [1]. A 2001 Stroke study found vertebrobasilar accidents were five times more likely in adults under 45 who had visited a chiropractor in the preceding week, with no significant association above 45 [1]. Some chiropractors dispute that manipulation causes these events [1].

A reported case of a young woman developed headache, vomiting, double vision, dizziness and ataxia after neck manipulation, and imaging showed a cerebellar infarct with fourth ventricle compression [2]. Another case report described multiple preretinal hemorrhages after cervical manipulation [3].
No studies found on neck adjustment for facial appearance. Studies of cervical manipulation address neck pain, and the safety literature consists largely of case reports and reviews [1][2][3].
